title: Si: anodized porous-silicon interposer cuts HBM link capacitance
idea: Electrochemically anodize the top 50-100 um of the silicon interposer into mesoporous Si (~60% porosity, k~2-3, very high effective resistivity) before building the RDL, so HBM-to-logic traces sit on a near-air dielectric instead of SiO2 over lossy doped Si. Anodization is a maskless wet bath step that fits existing 65 nm-class interposer lines.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~30-40% lower line capacitance and substrate loss, interposer I/O ~0.5 -> ~0.3 pJ/bit and ~2x reach so 12+ HBM stacks can ring one accelerator.

title: Al: anodic-alumina nanowire film replaces aligned microbumps for stacking
idea: Anodize aluminum into a 20-40 um AAO membrane with ~1e10 pores/cm2, electroplate Cu into the pores, and laminate it between dies as a z-axis-only conductor: any pad overlap conducts while lateral neighbors stay isolated, so die stacking needs only coarse (+/-5 um) placement yet reaches ~2-3 um effective pitch.
why: HBM bump/TSV tax and capital (fact 6): replaces multi-$M hybrid-bond aligners and CMP-critical surfaces with a wet anodization film; ~10x microbump density at a fraction of tool cost from abundant, US-sourced Al.

title: Ti: NiTi shape-memory micro-clamps make HBM stacks test-then-commit
idea: Pattern sputtered NiTi micro-spring fingers on interposer pads that stay open at room temperature and clamp onto HBM microbump arrays when warmed past Af (~70 C); the whole package is run at speed while clamped, bad stacks are released by cooling and swapped, and only then is permanent underfill/reflow committed.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): today one bad stack scraps a package carrying 8 stacks plus a GPU; demountable test-before-commit could recover most of the 20-30% compound yield loss, effectively +15-25% HBM supply.

title: Fe: magnetically steered parallel self-assembly of DRAM chiplets
idea: Deposit a patterned soft-magnetic Fe/Ni film on the back of each thinned DRAM chiplet and place an addressable electromagnet array beneath the target logic wafer in a fluid bath; thousands of chiplets settle and orient simultaneously into hybrid-bond sites with sub-um magnetic capture instead of serial pick-and-place.
why: Capital and throughput of die-to-wafer memory-on-logic bonding: from ~2k units/hour serial to >100k dies/hour per tool, cutting assembly cost ~5-10x.

title: Zn: ZnO piezo transducers send data acoustically through silicon stacks
idea: Sputter ZnO thin-film bulk-acoustic-wave transducers on every die so 1-5 GHz acoustic pulses carry data vertically through the bonded silicon stack (low acoustic loss in crystalline Si), with frequency-division channels per transducer; dies need a bonded acoustic path, not drilled and filled holes.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): hole-free stacking removes TSV keep-out zones and TSV yield loss; speculative ~0.5-1 pJ/bit links at modest per-channel rates.

title: C: polyethylene dielectric waveguides carry sub-THz memory traffic
idea: Drive 140-300 GHz carriers from plain CMOS transceivers into solid polyethylene/PTFE ribbon waveguides (cheap carbon-chain plastic, no lasers, no fiber alignment) between accelerator trays and memory sleds, each ribbon carrying 8-16 lanes at ~50-100 Gb/s.
why: Data-movement energy and stranded memory (fact 5): ~1 pJ/bit at 1-2 m vs ~5-10 pJ/bit for copper SerDes, making rack-level memory pooling cheap so less DRAM is provisioned per accelerator.

title: N: GaN micro-LED arrays form a wide-slow optical memory bus
idea: Bond 1,000-element GaN micro-LED emitter arrays and Si photodiode arrays to the memory controller and to a remote DRAM sled, each LED running 2-4 Gb/s NRZ into one core of an imaging fiber bundle, so the bus stays massively parallel and protocol-light like HBM instead of serializing.
why: Data movement (fact 5): sub-1 pJ/bit over 1-10 m with no SerDes or lasers, letting HBM-class bandwidth come from cheap off-package DRAM and avoiding the HBM TSV tax per accelerator.

title: O: IGZO-TFT active glass interposer hosts memory buffers and repeaters
idea: Fabricate InGaZnO oxide thin-film transistors (display-fab tooling, 1-10 um rules) directly on a glass interposer to implement repeaters, address buffers, ECC and power gating between logic and many DRAM dies, so the DRAM base die/PHY shrinks and the memory plane can span half a meter.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7) and capital (fact 4): moves logic onto Gen-8 display tools at ~1/100 the $/mm2 of silicon; enables panel-sized memory planes with distributed repeaters.

title: Na: ion-exchanged graded-index waveguides written into soda-lime interposers
idea: Exchange Na+ ions in soda-lime or aluminosilicate glass for K+/Ag+ through a patterned mask in a molten-salt bath, writing buried graded-index optical waveguides into the glass interposer itself to route light between co-packaged optics and memory chiplets.
why: Data-movement energy and capital: optical routing at display-glass cost with no silicon-photonics fab steps; panel-scale waveguides at cents per cm2 enable multi-stack optical memory fabrics.

title: Mg: MgB2 superconducting wiring links 20 K cryogenic memory pods
idea: Run DRAM pods at ~20 K (cryocooler or liquid hydrogen) and wire them to compute with MgB2 superconducting traces (Tc 39 K, made from abundant Mg and B) on flex/interposer, so long lines are lossless and drivers swing millivolts; at 20 K access-transistor leakage collapses and refresh nearly stops.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): link energy becomes almost distance-independent (~0.1 pJ/bit) and refresh power ~0; cryo overhead must be amortized over large pods.

title: Ca: calcium-gettered vacuum-gap interposer wiring with k equal to one
idea: Etch away the inter-line dielectric of interposer RDL to leave Cu lines suspended on posts, seal the package hermetically, and hold the gaps at high vacuum with an evaporated calcium getter film, giving k~1.0 and zero dielectric loss between memory lines.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): ~3-4x lower line capacitance than SiO2, interposer/HBM I/O energy down ~60% and higher bandwidth per mm of die edge.

title: S: Sb2S3 phase-change photonic crossbar pools memory across accelerators
idea: Use low-loss antimony-sulfide (Sb2S3) phase-change cells on silicon-nitride waveguides as non-volatile 2x2 switches in a 64x64 optical crossbar between accelerators and memory sleds; a route is set by one heater/laser pulse and then holds with zero static power, reassigning memory capacity per job.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: pooling typically recovers 20-40% of stranded provisioned DRAM; zero hold power makes per-job remapping cheap vs electrical switch fabrics.

title: Ba: barium-titanate Pockels modulators for femtojoule memory optics
idea: Bond thin-film epitaxial BaTiO3 (r42 ~900 pm/V, ~30x LiNbO3) onto silicon microrings so memory-link modulators switch with ~0.5 V and ~10 fF, driven directly from DRAM-process logic without driver amplifiers.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): optical memory I/O with ~50-100 fJ/bit modulator energy, making off-package memory cheaper per bit moved than HBM's 3-4 pJ/bit.

title: Sr: strontium-titanate pads give bumpless capacitive memory tiles
idea: Coat face-to-face I/O pads with a ~50 nm SrTiO3 film (k~300) so a DRAM chiplet laid face-down overlapping the logic die edge couples signals capacitively at 5-10 um pitch with no solder; tiles are held by a spring clip and can be re-seated or swapped.
why: HBM bump tax and rework (fact 6): contactless coupling at ~0.1 pJ/bit, no bumps to crack, and upgrade/repair without scrapping packages.

title: B: turn idle US borosilicate glass lines into interposer fabs
idea: Retool shuttered or underused US display/solar glass finishing lines to produce 510x515 mm borosilicate glass-core panels with laser-drilled through-glass vias for HBM packaging, using the existing US specialty-glass base instead of building new silicon interposer capacity.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (facts 4, 6): panels give ~5-8x the usable area of a 300 mm interposer wafer at a fraction of capex, breaking the CoWoS-style interposer bottleneck for HBM.

title: Er: erbium-amplified optical broadcast shares one weight copy
idea: Stream model weights from a single DRAM pool through an Er-doped waveguide-amplified 1-to-64 optical splitter tree, so every accelerator receives the same weight stream each step instead of each holding its own HBM copy; the amplifiers cancel the ~18 dB split loss.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: in data-parallel inference, weight replicas are often 50-80% of HBM contents; broadcast could cut total DRAM per cluster ~2-5x.

title: Ag: maskless inkjet-silver RDL for low-volume memory interposers
idea: Print redistribution layers with nano-silver ink sintered at ~150 C and inkjet-printed polyimide dielectric directly on glass or organic interposers at 5-10 um lines, so custom memory-chiplet interposers need no photomasks, steppers or plating lines.
why: Capital intensity (fact 4): removes ~$100k-1M mask sets per interposer design and litho tools; lets small U.S. firms build HBM-style packages in weeks.

title: Co: CoFeB spin-torque nano-oscillators as in-package memory radios
idea: Use CoFeB/MgO magnetic-tunnel-junction spin-torque nano-oscillators (~100 nm, 5-40 GHz, tuned by bias current) as frequency-agile transmitters and detectors, giving each DRAM die its own wireless channel inside a shielded package so dies can sit without TSVs or bumps.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and packaging capital: each oscillator uses <1 um2 vs ~100 um2 for a TSV plus keep-out; speculative 1-2 pJ/bit.

title: Si: deep-trench DRAM built into the passive interposer itself
idea: Interposers are thousands of mm2 of idle silicon: fabricate 1T1C eDRAM in them using the deep-trench capacitors (~30-60 fF, far above the ~5 fF pillar wall) that interposer lines already offer for decoupling, at 65-90 nm DUV rules, as a memory tier beside the HBM stacks.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1) and capital (fact 4): a 2,500 mm2 interposer could add ~1-2 GB of low-latency memory on fully depreciated DUV tools; large Cs also relaxes refresh.

title: Cu: copper-pillar bare DRAM dies soldered straight onto motherboards
idea: Flip-chip unpackaged DRAM dies with Cu pillars directly onto a motherboard region beside the CPU (chip-on-board, glob-topped), eliminating the BGA substrate, DIMM PCB and connector so memory traces shrink from ~10 cm to ~2 cm.
why: Cost per bit and energy: package/module overhead is ~10-15% of DIMM cost and long traces dominate DDR's 10-20 pJ/bit; ~2x lower I/O energy and no substrate supply dependency.

title: Ge: germanosilicate fiber delay loops hold model weights in flight
idea: Echoing mercury delay-line memory, circulate model weights as WDM light in a Ge-doped silica fiber loop (10 km ~ 50 us at 100 Tb/s ~ 600 MB in flight), re-amplified each lap and tapped at each accelerator exactly when the next layer needs those weights; the wire itself is the storage.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: weights are read cyclically every token, so sequential delay storage fits the access pattern; replaces GBs of HBM with fiber at cents per meter, energy set by amplification per lap.

title: W: tungsten-free contactless probing raises known-good-die for HBM
idea: Replace W/Re needle probe cards (China ~80% of tungsten) with inductive/capacitive coupling coils placed in the scribe line and die I/O, so DRAM core wafers are tested at full speed without touching pads, enabling at-speed known-good-die screening before stacking.
why: HBM yield (fact 6) and scarce resources: at-speed KGD could halve the 20-30% stack yield loss and removes a tungsten dependency plus pad damage that hurts hybrid bonding.

title: Si: unsawn wafer-scale DRAM bonded to wafer-scale compute
idea: Skip dicing: bond a whole DRAM wafer face-to-face to a whole logic wafer with reticle-stitched routing and a boot-time defect map that routes around bad DRAM dies, so die yield becomes capacity rather than scrap and no packages, interposers or TSVs exist.
why: Packaging cost and HBM tax (fact 6): ~1 TB+ per wafer pair at ~0.1 pJ/bit vertical links; a defective die just trims capacity instead of killing a stack.

title: Si: die-agnostic DDR5 buffer builds RDIMMs from any surplus die
idea: Put a silicon bridge buffer (extended RCD plus data buffers) on a standard DDR5 RDIMM that speaks JEDEC DDR5 to the host but drives LPDDR4X/LPDDR5, DDR4 or downbinned dies behind it, translating timing and bank structure, so modules can be assembled from whatever DRAM die is in surplus.
why: Usable supply with host interface unchanged: mobile and legacy DRAM inventories and mature DDR4 lines become server DDR5 capacity, adding several % of bits to the tightest market segment.

title: Al: wire-bonded stacks behind DDR5 buffers free TSV capacity
idea: Build 128-256 GB RDIMMs/MRDIMMs from 4-8-die staggered stacks connected with Al/Cu wire bonds (NAND-style) behind the module's data buffers instead of TSV-based 3DS; the buffers hide the stub loads so the host still sees a standard DDR5 module.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): TSV and stacking capacity is the HBM chokepoint; moving high-capacity server DIMMs off TSVs frees it for HBM at near-zero new capex.

title: Ti: rutile-TiO2 trench decoupling under the HBM PHY
idea: Line interposer and base-die deep-trench capacitors with rutile TiO2 (k~80-110, templated on RuO2) instead of HfO2/ZrO2 (k~25-40), tripling decap density directly under the HBM PHY and TSV power columns.
why: Speed-bin yield at an unchanged HBM interface: supply droop is a leading reason stacks miss top speed; ~3x decap cuts droop and could raise good-stack output ~5-10%.

title: Fe: magnetite-loaded underfill enables induction rework of one HBM stack
idea: Load HBM underfill and joint regions with Fe3O4 nanoparticles so a localized RF coil heats only the failing stack's joints to reflow, lifting and replacing it while the GPU and seven neighbors stay below ~100 C; package and interface are unchanged.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): rework instead of scrapping very expensive multi-stack packages; recovers the ~10-20% of packages that fail final test because of a single stack.

title: Zn: ZnO thin-film varistors move DRAM ESD into the package
idea: Embed ZnO multilayer varistor arrays in the DRAM package substrate under each DQ/CA ball to clamp assembly ESD, letting the die's own ESD diodes and pad structures shrink to CDM minimum while still meeting JEDEC pin capacitance and drive specs.
why: Periphery ~49% of die (fact 7): I/O and ESD rings are several % of die area and add pin capacitance; shrinking them yields ~2-4% more dies per wafer and lower I/O energy at the same interface.

title: Sn: self-healing Sn-In microbumps reflowed by on-die heaters
idea: Replace SnAg microbumps in HBM stacks with Sn-In eutectic (118 C) and add polysilicon microheaters beside bump fields; when base-die link training detects rising error rates or resistance, the stack is reflowed in place during a maintenance window to heal thermo-mechanical cracks.
why: HBM field reliability and effective supply: bump cracks drive RMAs and spare provisioning; in-situ repair extends stack life and could cut replacement demand ~10%.

title: C: CVD-diamond interleaf shims keep HBM below refresh-doubling heat
idea: Bond 20-30 um polycrystalline CVD diamond layers (1,000-1,500 W/m-K) into HBM/3DS stacks every four dies, with laser-drilled through-diamond vias, so base-die and core-die heat spreads laterally to the lid; the electrical interface is untouched.
why: Refresh (fact 3): above 85 C DRAM must refresh 2x, costing energy and ~10-20% bandwidth; a 10-15 C cooler stack avoids it and lets 16-20-high stacks stay in spec.

title: N: silicon-nitride linear-drive optics extend DDR5 slots off-board
idea: Insert a linear, non-retimed optical extender at each DDR5 socket: Si3N4/SiP modulators driven directly by the DQ/DQS analog waveforms and photodiodes at a remote liquid-cooled DIMM tray 0.3-1 m away, with the host's existing read/write leveling absorbing the extra ~3-5 ns flight time.
why: Capacity per socket and data movement with interface unchanged: DIMMs leave the crowded board, allowing 2-4x more DIMMs per CPU and better cooling, at ~2-4 pJ/bit added.

title: Mg: magnesium-silicide thermoelectric micro-coolers spot-cool HBM PHY
idea: Integrate thin-film Mg2Si/Mg3Sb2 Peltier elements (abundant, tellurium-free alternative to Bi2Te3) in the HBM lid over the hottest base-die PHY region, actively pumping 5-10 W/cm2 during bursts so the stack never crosses 85 C; control is local and the interface unchanged.
why: Refresh and throttling (fact 3): avoids 2x refresh and thermal throttling at peak load using abundant elements with no Te/China chokepoint.

title: Ga: GaN single-stage 48V-to-VDDQ regulation at the memory
idea: Mount GaN-FET hybrid switched-capacitor converters on the package substrate (and on DDR5 DIMMs in place of the 12 V PMIC) converting 48 V straight to VDD/VDDQ for the DRAM, eliminating an intermediate bus-conversion stage.
why: Energy per bit at system level: memory power delivery loses ~10-15% across two stages; single-stage GaN recovers ~5-8 points and cuts board copper, with DRAM interfaces unchanged.

title: Hf: HfO2 antifuse farms enable massive post-stack HBM repair
idea: Add a dense HfO2-breakdown antifuse array (1T1AF, ~0.1 um2 each) to the HBM base die that remaps failing core-die rows, columns and whole sub-banks found after stacking and at-speed test, far beyond today's limited post-package repair fuses.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): defects discovered after bonding are the main 20-30% loss; 10-100x more repair elements could recover a large share with zero host change.

title: Cu: hybrid-bonded 16-high DDR5 3DS stacks in standard packages
idea: Use Cu-Cu/oxide hybrid bonding (no microbumps, no underfill) to stack 16 thinned DDR5 dies within today's 3DS package height, keeping the standard DDR5 3DS ballout and RDIMM interface.
why: Density per module: 2x dies per package at the same height gives 512 GB RDIMMs from existing dies, with lower stack thermal resistance.

title: Mo: molybdenum-filled TSVs shrink keep-out zones in HBM dies
idea: Fill HBM core-die TSVs with molybdenum (CTE 4.8 ppm/K vs Cu 17, Si 2.6) instead of copper, cutting thermo-mechanical stress so the transistor keep-out zone around each TSV shrinks from ~5-10 um to ~1-2 um and Cu pumping disappears.
why: HBM TSV area tax (fact 6): reclaims ~3-5% core-die area and reduces TSV-related yield loss with the HBM interface unchanged; avoids tungsten fill and its China chokepoint.

title: Li: beta-eucryptite negative-expansion filler stops HBM package warpage
idea: Replace part of the fused-silica filler in mold compound and underfill with beta-eucryptite (LiAlSiO4, CTE ~ -6 ppm/K, from abundant Li, Al, Si) to bring composite CTE to ~3 ppm/K matching silicon, eliminating warpage of 8-12-stack HBM packages.
why: HBM packaging yield and size: warpage limits interposer size and causes bump opens; CTE matching allows more stacks per package and reduces high-purity fused-quartz filler demand.

title: Co: cobalt-alloy magnetic-core coils replace signal TSVs inside HBM
idea: Inside the stack, couple core dies inductively with on-die coils wrapped around electroplated CoFe/CoZrTa thin-film magnetic cores (relative permeability ~500), boosting coupling through 20-30 um thinned dies so signal paths need no TSVs; the base die still presents the standard HBM PHY.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes signal-TSV area, keep-out and TSV yield loss at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit; only a few large power TSVs remain.

title: Ge-Sn: group-IV emitters beam data vertically through HBM dies
idea: Grow GeSn light emitters at ~2 um wavelength (where silicon is transparent) and matching GeSn photodiodes on each core die so bit lanes pass optically straight through the thinned stack, dropping signal TSVs; the base die converts to the unchanged HBM interface.
why: HBM TSV tax and yield (fact 6): optical vertical channels avoid TSV keep-out and alignment loss while staying CMOS-compatible; speculative ~1 pJ/bit.

title: Ni: electroless-nickel sidewall wiring replaces TSVs in die stacks
idea: Route HBM core-die I/O to the die edge, stack the dies, then laser-pattern and electrolessly plate Ni/Cu/Au traces down the polished stack sidewall at ~10 um pitch (~4,000 lines on a 10 mm die perimeter) to the base die, which keeps the standard HBM PHY.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): core dies need no TSVs, keep-outs or backside processing, saving ~5-10% die area and improving stack yield.

title: Au: right-to-reuse rule stops shredding retired server DIMMs
idea: Policy: require hyperscalers and IT-asset recyclers to route retired DDR4/DDR5 server DIMMs through certified re-test and resale before any gold-recovery shredding, with a per-GB reuse tax credit; reused modules drop into existing DDR slots unchanged.
why: Usable memory supply: retired fleet DRAM is a large stranded pool currently destroyed for grams of gold; reuse could add several % of annual bit supply at near-zero capex.

title: F: PTFE-laminate channels enable full-speed two-DIMMs-per-channel DDR5
idea: Route server DDR5 channels and DIMM risers on PTFE/fluoropolymer laminate (Df ~0.001 vs ~0.01-0.02 for FR-4 class) so two-DIMMs-per-channel topologies keep DDR5-6400 instead of derating to ~4400.
why: Capacity per socket at unchanged interface: doubles DIMM count per channel without a speed penalty, so lower-density, more available DIMMs can meet capacity targets.

title: K: KNN piezo chuck actively flattens interposers during HBM bonding
idea: Embed lead-free (K,Na)NbO3 piezo actuator arrays in the bonding chuck that measure and counter-bend large interposers in real time during HBM thermocompression or reflow, holding coplanarity under 5 um across ~100 mm packages.
why: HBM packaging yield and size: warpage-driven non-wet opens cap interposer size and yield; active flattening allows larger multi-HBM packages with ~5-10% fewer assembly fallouts.

title: H: high-pressure deuterium anneal of finished stacks tightens retention
idea: Anneal completed HBM/3DS stacks in ~20 atm D2 at 250-300 C (within microbump limits) so deuterium diffuses to passivate Si/SiO2 interface traps in access transistors that drive trap-assisted leakage; the heavier isotope resists later hot-carrier depassivation.
why: Leakage tail (fact 3): fewer weak cells means more stacks pass 32/64 ms retention at 85-95 C and fewer repair elements consumed, ~3-5% yield gain with interface unchanged.

title: Na: sodium-silicate geopolymer encapsulant replaces epoxy around HBM stacks
idea: Fill and encapsulate HBM stacks with a low-temperature (~80 C cure) sodium-silicate aluminosilicate geopolymer loaded with AlN, giving an inorganic mold with CTE ~6-8 ppm/K, ~3-5 W/m-K and no outgassing; package outline and ballout stay unchanged.
why: Thermal and warpage (facts 3, 6): ~5-10x the conductivity of epoxy mold underfill lowers stack temperature and warpage, enabling taller stacks from abundant Na, Al, Si.

title: O: IGZO gain-cell row cache in HBM base die
idea: Add a few MB of IGZO 2T0C gain-cell memory (BEOL, seconds-scale retention, non-destructive read) on the HBM base die that caches recently opened core-die rows; repeat activations to cached rows are served from the base die with standard HBM timings, so core dies are not re-activated.
why: Destructive read/overfetch (fact 8) and row hammer (fact 9): fewer core activations cut internal energy ~20-30% on reuse-heavy traffic and dilute hammering, all behind the standard HBM protocol.
